catalog_quote: [p. 167] § 2. — Accent et ton. Le profil musical de certains mots est le même qu'en Nenema: l'expression: ni apulip = les hommes, dite isolée, donne une courbe pareille à celle de: axamale (cf. sup. p. 128). Cette intonation confirme la tradition qui fait peupler les Belep par une forte émigration de Gatope. Mais, hors [p. 168] ces mots isolés et prononcés de la sorte, le profil même de la phrase demeure uniforme et martelé, des mots très longs exigeant un débit très rapide. new_statements.translation: § 2. — Accent and tone. The musical profile of certain words is the same as in Nenema: the expression ni apulip = 'the men', said in isolation, gives a curve like that of axamale (cf. above p. 128). This intonation confirms the tradition that the Belep were peopled by a strong emigration from Gatope. But, apart from these isolated words pronounced in that way, the profile of the phrase itself remains uniform and hammered, very long words requiring a very rapid delivery.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-stress placement is given. Leenhardt describes prosody only at the phrase level: a uniform, 'hammered' (evenly beaten) phrase contour with no prominent word accent, except that certain words said in isolation carry a characteristic melodic curve like the one he draws for Nenema (where he says the phrase unfolds 'sans accents marqués'). No accent marks appear on any Haveke word in the chapter.
new_statements.exceptions: Certain words pronounced in isolation (e.g. ni apulip 'the men') show a Nenema-like pitch curve; otherwise none.
new_statements.domain_note: Phrase-level impressionistic description (1946, pre-phonemic survey sketch); isolated citation forms vs. connected phrase are contrasted. No instrumental or phonological analysis. Rivierre 1972 (p. 302) classes the Voh-Koné dialects incl. Haveke as toneless.
new_statements.identity_note: Leenhardt's "'Avekè" (ch. 30; Ilot de Gatope, Webione, Voh; 100 speakers in 1946) = Haveke [have1241] (Glottolog lists Leenhardt 1946 as have1241's sole Glottolog's most extensive description; Rivierre's Voh-Koné fiche equates 'Aveké no.30 with haveke, now spoken at Oudjo/Oundjo and Gatope, 421 speakers). Rivierre & Ehrhart 2006 treat 'haveke' (Oundjo, consultant Elan Dianaï) as one of three dialects alongside bwatoo [bwat1240] and haeke [haek1239]; ISO 639-3 CR 2012-143 rejected an update to [hvk]; en.wikipedia 'Haveke language' redirects to Bwatoo. Do not confuse with Hmwaveke [hmwa1243] ('Moaveke, Tiéta).

sources.note: §2 'Accent et ton': the musical profile of certain words is the same as in Nenema (ni apulip 'the men' said in isolation has a curve like Nenema axamale, p.128); apart from such isolated words 'le profil même de la phrase demeure uniforme et martelé, des mots très longs exigeant un débit très rapide'. No word-stress placement rule; no accent marks on the word examples in §3. The cross-referenced Nenema §2 says 'La phrase se déroule sans accents marqués, mais avec une courbe musicale caractéristique'.
